We explore this survey together, one step at a time, the way you would explore any new
data: start at the source, learn how it was collected, load it, look at its shape, then
play with it and plot it. The last step answers one question with `lm()`.

Almost everything here you have used in Classes 4–7. The new things are all about text:
putting text in order, turning text into numbers, and searching inside text.

---

# 1. Start at the source

Before you open R, find out what the data is and where it came from.

- **The data:** GigaDB, <https://doi.org/10.5524/102783>
- **The article that describes it:** Sriwichai et al. (2026), *AI in practice: a
  multilingual survey of 2025 BioHackathon participants*, GigaByte,
  <https://doi.org/10.46471/gigabyte.179>

*Your turn:* open both pages. Who answered? How were they asked? In which languages? How
many answered?

What the pages say:

- **Who:** participants and community members around the 2025 BioHackathon in Japan.
- **How:** a Google Form, anonymous, in English, Japanese or Thai. 105 people submitted it.
- **Optional:** almost every question. Only the language and the question on how often
  you use AI had to be answered.
- **Not shown to everyone:** some questions appeared only after certain answers.

The answers are free to reuse for any purpose (CC0). The article sums them up in one
figure, one question at a time:

![](https://gigabytejournal.com/admin/apis/public/article_shell/uploads/article_files/Gigabyte/Gigabyte/2026/gigabyte179/gigabyte-2026-179-g001.jpg)

<small>Figure 1 of Sriwichai et al. (2026), GigaByte, CC BY 4.0.</small>

The files are in `data/survey/` in your SIRE516 project folder (the one with
`SIRE516.Rproj`), unchanged from GigaDB. If your folder has no `data/survey/`, download the
course folder again (the README, step 3) into a new folder, and work in the new one from
now on. Three files
matter most:

| File | What it holds |
|---|---|
| `…_data_cleaned_ENG_R1.csv` | One row per person, in English. **The table you analyse.** |
| `…_cleaned_codebook_ENG_R1.csv` | What each column of that table means |
| `…_GoogleForms.pdf` | The questionnaire: every question, every option, and which question each person was sent to next |

**Open the questionnaire PDF and the codebook now, and keep them open,** from RStudio's
Files pane or from your computer's file browser. When a cell in the table is blank, the
questionnaire is how you find out whether that person was ever shown the question.

---

# 2. Load it, and look at its shape

*Predict:* the form had 105 answers. How many rows should the table have, and what is one
row?

```{r}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)

survey <- read_csv("data/survey/Biohackathon2025AISurvey_data_cleaned_ENG_R1.csv",
                   show_col_types = FALSE)
dim(survey)
```

105 rows: one person each. Each column holds the answers to one question, or to one part
of a question. Look at all 33:

```{r}
glimpse(survey)
```

27 columns are text (`<chr>`) and 6 are numbers (`<dbl>`): the satisfaction score, the
support score, and four of the five `concern_` scores.

*Predict:* the five `concern_` columns are all scores from 1 to 5. Why is
`concern_misinfo` text? Section 5 answers it.

---

# 3. One column at a time

`table()` from Class 4 counts each value. Add `useNA = "ifany"` and it counts the blanks
(`NA` in R) too, which in a survey is half the story.

```{r}
table(survey$ai_use_level, useNA = "ifany")
```

61 people use AI every day; one never does. Every value is spelled as the form wrote it,
with one surprise: look closely at `I am an Al researcher` and `I use Al a few times a
month`. That is *Al*, with a lower-case L, not *AI*. In many fonts the two look the same.
Section 4 shows why it matters.

Where people work:

```{r}
table(survey$country, useNA = "ifany")
```

14 values, one of them *Global*, and 6 blanks. 44 people work in Japan and 23 in Thailand,
so a comparison between countries is, in practice, Japan against Thailand:

```{r}
sum(survey$country %in% c("Japan", "Thailand"))
```

67 of 105. Why are 6 blank? Country was optional and typed by hand. 5 people skipped it,
and the authors' cleaning (`README_R1.md`) blanked one answer that was not a country.

*Your turn:* count `age` and `gender`, blanks included.

```{r}

```

## A cell with several answers

Some questions said *tick all that apply*. Their cells hold every box a person ticked,
joined by commas:

```{r}
head(survey$challenges_faced, 3)
```

To ask *did this person tick this box?*, search the text. `grepl("inaccurate", x)` gives
TRUE where `x` contains *inaccurate* and FALSE where it does not. A blank gives FALSE.
Search for a short, plain word that only that box contains. The word must appear exactly
as you type it, capitals included, and leave out brackets: they mean something special to
`grepl()`. (Note *Al outputs*
above: the *Al* spelling is in these cells too.)

```{r}
survey <- survey |>
  mutate(inaccurate = grepl("inaccurate", challenges_faced))

table(survey$inaccurate)
sum(is.na(survey$challenges_faced))
```

77 ticked it. But 4 people have no answer, and they are counted in the 28 FALSE too. One of
them is the person who never uses AI, whom the form never showed this question. Decide what
a blank means before you compare the groups. (Do not split the cells at their commas: some
answers contain a comma themselves, such as *Data limitations (size, quality,
accessibility)*.)

---

# 4. Text in order: factors

Plot how often people use AI. Put the column on `y`, so the long labels fit:

```{r}
ggplot(survey, aes(y = ai_use_level)) +
  geom_bar()
```

The bars are in alphabetical order, which tells you nothing. To choose the order, turn the
column into a **factor**: text with a fixed list of values, its *levels*, in the order you
give. `factor(x, levels = ...)` makes one. Type the levels as the questionnaire words them,
in the order you want the bars from the bottom up: *never*, the developer, the researcher,
then monthly, weekly and every day.

*Predict:* every person should land in one of the seven levels. Will any be `NA`?

```{r}
typed <- c("I never use AI", "I am an AI developer", "I am an AI researcher",
           "I use AI a few times a month", "I use AI a few times a week",
           "I use AI everyday", "Other")

table(factor(survey$ai_use_level, levels = typed), useNA = "ifany")
```

14 people became `NA`, and nothing warned you: a value that does not match a level
**exactly** becomes `NA`. The 6 researchers and the 8 monthly users are spelled *Al* in
the data. Copy the levels from the data, never from the questionnaire:

```{r}
use_levels <- c("I never use AI", "I am an AI developer",
                "I am an Al researcher",            # Al, lower-case L, as in the data
                "I use Al a few times a month",     # here too
                "I use AI a few times a week", "I use AI everyday", "Other")

survey <- survey |>
  mutate(use = factor(ai_use_level, levels = use_levels))

table(survey$use, useNA = "ifany")

ggplot(survey, aes(y = use)) +
  geom_bar()
```

No `NA`, and the bars run in order. A plot draws the first level next to where the two
axes meet, so on a `y` axis *never* is at the bottom.

---

# 5. Text into numbers

Back to `concern_misinfo`:

```{r}
table(survey$concern_misinfo, useNA = "ifany")
```

Two answers kept their labels: *5 - Very concerned* and *1 - Not concerned at all*. Every
value in a column has one type (Class 4), so one piece of text makes the whole column
text, and `mean()` gives up:

```{r}
mean(survey$concern_misinfo, na.rm = TRUE)
```

`parse_number()`, from `readr`, keeps the number at the start of each value:

```{r}
survey <- survey |>
  mutate(concern_misinfo = parse_number(concern_misinfo))

table(survey$concern_misinfo, useNA = "ifany")
```

Now look at the other four concerns the same way:

```{r}
table(survey$concern_bias, useNA = "ifany")
table(survey$concern_privacy, useNA = "ifany")
table(survey$concern_ip, useNA = "ifany")
table(survey$concern_environment, useNA = "ifany")
```

*Predict:* what is missing from all four?

**No 1s and no 5s at all**, and 29 to 41 blanks each. Misinformation, asked in the same
grid on the form, has 49 fives and only 10 blanks. The likeliest reading is that answers
at the two ends of the scale were lost before the file was published, and became blanks.
The files cannot prove it, but it means these four columns cannot give you a mean or a
comparison you can defend. Leave them out of your project.

Misinformation is not clean either. The file of answers in their original languages
(`…_original_languages_R1.csv`) shows
that the 20 people who answered on the Thai form gave it no 1s or 5s, and left 9 of its 10
blanks. Its mean is mostly English and Japanese answers, and comparing it between
countries partly compares the forms.

---

# 6. Plot, and explore

Satisfaction with AI, from 1 to 5:

```{r}
table(survey$satisfaction_score, useNA = "ifany")

ggplot(survey, aes(x = satisfaction_score)) +
  geom_bar()
```

Most people are satisfied: 69 of 104 gave a 4 or a 5. The warning, *Removed 1 row*, is
the 105th person: the one who never uses AI, whom the form never asked about satisfaction.

Some blanks are there by design. Question 18, *what would AI tools need to improve*, was
skipped for people who rated their satisfaction 4 or 5. Check it with a two-way
`table()`, as in Class 4:

```{r}
table(survey$satisfaction_score, is.na(survey$improvements_desired), useNA = "ifany")
```

`TRUE` means blank. Everyone who gave a 4 or a 5 is blank, because nobody who gave a 4 or
a 5 saw the question. Check the questionnaire before you read a blank as anything.

Now two columns together. Does satisfaction look different by how often people use AI?

```{r, fig.height = 6}
ggplot(survey, aes(x = satisfaction_score)) +
  geom_bar() +
  facet_wrap(~ use)
```

*Predict:* which group looks most satisfied? Which groups are too small to say? (The
*never* panel is empty for the same reason as the warning.)

*Your turn:* draw `inst_support_score` the same way, one panel per `use`.

# 7. One question, answered with `lm()`

> Are people who use AI every day more satisfied with it than people who use it a few
> times a week?

Keep those two groups, and look before you model:

```{r}
two <- survey |>
  filter(ai_use_level %in% c("I use AI a few times a week", "I use AI everyday"))

table(two$ai_use_level)

ggplot(two, aes(x = satisfaction_score)) +
  geom_bar() +
  facet_wrap(~ ai_use_level, ncol = 1)
```

`ncol = 1` stacks the two panels in one column, so their bars line up. 23 weekly users, 61
daily ones. The daily users pile up at 4 and 5. Now the model, as in Class 7:

```{r}
fit <- lm(satisfaction_score ~ ai_use_level, data = two)
summary(fit)
confint(fit)
```

The baseline is the weekly group: in alphabetical order, *a few times a week* comes
before *everyday* (Class 7, section 4). So *everyday* is 1 for daily users and 0 for weekly
ones:

> satisfaction = 3.30 + 0.79 × everyday

Weekly users average 3.30; daily users average 0.79 points more. Report it, estimate and
interval first:

> People who use AI every day rated their satisfaction 0.79 points higher, on average,
> than people who use it a few times a week (95% CI 0.41 to 1.18; p = 0.00008).

Then read it honestly, as in Class 7:

- **A comparison, not a cause.** Nobody was assigned how often to use AI. People who like
  it may simply use it more.
- **The same spread in both groups?** The model assumes it, but the weekly group is smaller
  and spreads more. Welch's test, `t.test()`'s default in Class 7, does not assume it (see
  below).
- **The score is treated as a number,** as if the step from 3 to 4 were the same size as
  the step from 4 to 5.
- **The question came after the look.** We picked it after the plot in section 6, so treat
  the answer as a lead. In your project, decide the question first (Class 7, section 8).
- **Who answered.** 84 volunteers around one hackathon, not bioinformaticians in general.

Welch's test:

```{r}
t.test(satisfaction_score ~ ai_use_level, data = two)
```

The interval has its signs flipped, as in Class 7, section 4: `t.test()` takes the first
group minus the second, weekly minus daily. Turned round, it is 0.36 to 1.23 points, with
p = 0.0008: wider, and the same conclusion. Say which one you report.

That is the whole shape of your project: a question, a look, two figures, a model, and the
story.

---

# 8. Where to take it

Questions this table can support:

- Are people with more support from their institution more satisfied with AI?
- Is institutional support different in Japan and in Thailand? (Keep in mind the forms,
  below.)
- Do the people who ticked *outputs are inaccurate or unreliable* rate their satisfaction
  lower?

Before you choose, know what this table is:

- **105 people who chose to answer**, around one hackathon.
- **Small groups.** 6 AI researchers, 4 developers, 1 person who never uses AI.
- **Almost every question optional.** Count the blanks in every column you use, and check
  the questionnaire for why they are there.
- **The concern columns** (section 5): four without 1s or 5s, and misinformation without
  them on the Thai form.
- **Country and form go together.** The original-language file shows that 16 of the 23
  people in Thailand answered on the Thai form, so a difference between countries may
  partly be a difference between forms.

> **Before you trust a summary of this survey, look at the answers under it.**
